prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- The fiery leader of Lebanon's Hezbollah militant movement assured Lebanon on Monday that his movement will cooperate in the country's political life. Supporters carry posters of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah. Hassan Nasrallah said: "We don't want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon or to impose our ideas over the people of Lebanon, because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone." Nasrallah spoke a day after Lebanon's parliament elected Michel Sleiman the country's president after a six-month vacancy in the position. Nasrallah, speaking at a packed stadium, told his followers: "I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions. The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese." He said Sleiman's election "renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start." "I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs, we are both in front of two choices; either to expand the wounds and add salt to them or try to cure them for the sake of Lebanon and we prefer the second choice." The parliament had tried 19 times to vote on a new president, but failed because of disagreements over how to share power in a new Cabinet. Lebanon's Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached a deal last week aimed at ending an 18-month political crisis that pushed the country to the brink of civil war, and paved the way for Sleiman's election. The agreement, reached in Doha, Qatar, calls for a consensus government in which the Cabinet would be comprised of 30 posts -- 16 for the majority, 11 for the Hezbollah-led opposition and three set aside for the president to nominate. The seat allocation had been a key sticking point for the opposition, which wanted to ensure it had the power to veto major decisions. With 11 Cabinet posts, it will have that power. In exchange for the veto power and a redistricting plan ahead of next year's elections, Hezbollah agreed to end its sit-in protest that has paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006. In his speech, Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and to the Arab League for helping broker the deal. Sleiman was the consensus candidate, and is viewed as a neutral party by Lebanon's political factions. The nation's previous presidents have been seen as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western. In his 10 years as chief of the army, Sleiman also is believed to have unified the splintered military. However, he inherits a nation grappling with divisions. Lebanon's elected, pro-Western government has long been locked in a power struggle with Hezbollah. In public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah threatened to use its power and popularity to oust the Sunni-led government, triggering fears of a new civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region. The election helped end a political crisis that deteriorated into violence this month. That crisis was defused when the Lebanese government gave in to two key Hezbollah demands -- lifting a government ban of Hezbollah's telecommunications system and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut's airport. "The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions," Nasrallah said. "I promise that the opposition's representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares - and unfortunately we must speak of shares - even if it is at the expense of Hezbollah's shares." Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against U.S., Israeli, and other Western targets and the United States lists it as a terrorist organization. But many in Lebanon and other parts of the Middle East -- particularly Shiites -- view Hezbollah militants as freedom fighters.

**BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN)** — The fiery leader of Lebanon’s militant Hezbollah movement assured the nation Monday that his group would cooperate in the country’s political life.

Supporters carried posters of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah as he addressed a packed stadium.

“We don’t want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon or to impose our ideas over the people of Lebanon, because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone,” Nasrallah said.

He spoke one day after Lebanon’s parliament elected Michel Sleiman as the country’s president, filling a position that had been vacant for six months.

“I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions,” Nasrallah told his followers. “The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese.”

He said Sleiman’s election “renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start.”

“I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs,” Nasrallah said. “We are both in front of two choices: either to expand the wounds and add salt to them or try to cure them for the sake of Lebanon, and we prefer the second choice.”

Parliament had tried and failed 19 times to elect a new president because of disagreements over how power would be shared in a new Cabinet.

Lebanon’s Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached an agreement last week aimed at ending an 18-month political crisis that had pushed the country to the brink of civil war. The deal also paved the way for Sleiman’s election.

The agreement, reached in Doha, Qatar, calls for a consensus government with a 30-member Cabinet: 16 posts for the majority, 11 for the Hezbollah-led opposition and three to be filled by presidential nominees.

The allocation of Cabinet seats had been a key sticking point for the opposition, which wanted to ensure that it could veto major decisions. With 11 Cabinet posts, it will have that power.

In exchange for veto power and a redistricting plan ahead of next year’s elections, Hezbollah agreed to end the sit-in protest that had paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006.

In his speech, Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and the Arab League for helping broker the agreement.

Sleiman was the consensus candidate and is viewed as neutral by Lebanon’s political factions. The country’s previous presidents have been regarded as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western. During his 10 years as army chief, Sleiman is also believed to have unified the splintered military.

However, he inherits a nation still grappling with deep divisions.

Lebanon’s elected, pro-Western government has long been locked in a power struggle with Hezbollah. In public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah threatened to use its power and popularity to oust the Sunni-led government, prompting fears of a new civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region.

The election helped end a political crisis that descended into violence this month. The crisis was defused after the Lebanese government yielded to two key Hezbollah demands: lifting a government ban on Hezbollah’s telecommunications system and reinstating the security chief at Beirut’s airport.

“The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions,” Nasrallah said.

“I promise that the opposition’s representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares—and unfortunately we must speak of shares—even if it is at the expense of Hezbollah’s shares.”

Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against U.S., Israeli and other Western targets, and the United States lists it as a terrorist organization. However, many people in Lebanon and elsewhere in the Middle East—particularly Shiites—view Hezbollah militants as freedom fighters.

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) — Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah said Monday that the militant group intends to participate cooperatively in Lebanon’s political system.

Addressing followers in a crowded stadium, as supporters displayed posters bearing his image, Nasrallah said Hezbollah had no desire to dominate Lebanon, govern the country, or force its beliefs on the population. He described Lebanon as a uniquely diverse nation that can function only through cooperation among all its communities.

His remarks came one day after Parliament chose Michel Sleiman as president, filling an office that had remained vacant for six months.

Nasrallah renewed his call for genuine power-sharing without excluding any group or imposing one side’s will on another. He said the proposed national unity government should not be viewed as an opposition triumph over the governing coalition, but as a success for the entire Lebanese population.

According to Nasrallah, Sleiman’s election restored hope that Lebanon could enter a new period and make a fresh beginning. He acknowledged that both political camps had suffered serious wounds and said they now faced a choice: deepen those injuries or work to heal them for Lebanon’s benefit. Hezbollah, he said, favored reconciliation.

Lawmakers had made 19 unsuccessful attempts to elect a president, with disputes over the distribution of power in a new Cabinet preventing agreement.

The breakthrough came after Lebanon’s Western-supported government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached an accord the previous week. The deal was intended to resolve an 18-month political confrontation that had brought the country close to civil war and cleared the way for Sleiman’s election.

Negotiated in Doha, Qatar, the agreement established a 30-member consensus Cabinet. The parliamentary majority would receive 16 positions, the Hezbollah-led opposition would hold 11, and the president would choose the remaining three ministers.

Cabinet representation had been one of the opposition’s main concerns because it wanted enough seats to block major government actions. Holding 11 ministries gives it that veto authority.

In return for veto power and an electoral redistricting arrangement ahead of the following year’s elections, Hezbollah agreed to halt the sit-in that had largely shut down central Beirut since late 2006.

During his own address, Sleiman thanked Qatar and the Arab League for their roles in negotiating the agreement.

Sleiman emerged as the compromise choice for president and was regarded as neutral by Lebanon’s competing political groups. Previous presidents had generally been considered aligned either with Syria or with Western countries.

He was also credited with bringing unity to Lebanon’s fragmented armed forces during his decade as army commander. Nevertheless, he assumed the presidency of a country still burdened by severe political divisions.

Lebanon’s elected, pro-Western administration had been engaged for years in a struggle for influence with Hezbollah. Through public declarations and demonstrations, Hezbollah had threatened to use its strength and popular support to remove the Sunni-led government. Those threats fueled concerns that another civil war might erupt and further unsettle an already unstable region.

The presidential vote helped bring to a close a political dispute that had turned violent earlier that month. Tensions eased after the government accepted two central Hezbollah demands: it reversed a ban targeting Hezbollah’s telecommunications network and restored Beirut airport’s security chief to his position.

Nasrallah argued that the opposition’s conduct demonstrated it had not been attempting a coup. Instead, he said, its goal had been to compel what he called an illegitimate government to cancel those two measures.

He also promised that opposition seats in the new Cabinet would not be controlled exclusively by Hezbollah, Amal, and the Change and Reform bloc. Other opposition organizations would receive positions as well, he said, even if Hezbollah had to surrender some of its own allocation. He expressed regret that political representation had to be discussed in terms of dividing up shares.

Hezbollah has been associated with numerous terrorist attacks against American, Israeli, and other Western targets, and the U.S. government designates the organization as a terrorist group. However, many people in Lebanon and elsewhere in the Middle East—especially members of Shiite communities—regard Hezbollah’s fighters as participants in a liberation struggle.

**BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN)** — Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah pledged political cooperation following the election of army chief Michel Sleiman as Lebanon’s president, a vote made possible by a power-sharing agreement reached in Doha, Qatar.

In a televised address, Nasrallah welcomed Sleiman’s election and said Hezbollah and its political allies would work with the new president and Lebanon’s incoming national unity government.

Lebanon’s parliament elected Sleiman on May 25, 2008, ending an 18-month political crisis that had left the presidency vacant since November. His election followed an Arab-brokered agreement between the Western-backed governing coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition.

Under the Doha accord, the parties agreed to form a 30-member Cabinet in which the opposition would hold 11 seats—enough to block major government decisions. The deal also set out a new electoral law and called for dialogue on national security issues.

The agreement came after days of deadly fighting in Beirut and other parts of Lebanon, the country’s worst internal violence since the end of its civil war in 1990.

Nasrallah described the settlement as a chance to restore stability and political partnership. However, deep divisions remained over Hezbollah’s weapons and the organization’s independent military role—issues expected to be addressed in talks led by Sleiman.

Sleiman, viewed as a consensus figure, called on Lebanon’s rival factions to work together and strengthen state institutions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the May 2008 political developments in Lebanon, including Nasrallah’s unity speech, Sleiman’s election, and the Cabinet deal between Hezbollah and the Western-backed government.
counterfactuals.output:
- **Early-May clashes:** Lebanon’s Western-backed government moved against Hezbollah’s private telecommunications network and removed the Beirut airport security chief, whom it regarded as close to the group. Hezbollah called the decisions an attack on the resistance. Fighting erupted on May 7, and Hezbollah and allied gunmen briefly took control of much of western Beirut. Dozens were killed before the army and Arab mediation helped calm the crisis.

- **Doha Agreement:** After negotiations in Qatar, Lebanon’s rival factions signed the **May 21 Doha Agreement**. They agreed to end the violence, elect a president, form a national-unity government, adopt a revised election law, and refrain from using arms to settle domestic political disputes.

- **Sleiman’s election:** On **May 25**, parliament elected army commander **Gen. Michel Sleiman** president, filling an office that had been vacant since November 2007. His selection was presented as a compromise and a step toward restoring functioning state institutions.

- **Nasrallah’s unity speech:** The following day, Hezbollah leader **Hassan Nasrallah** struck a conciliatory tone, saying the crisis should have **“no victor and no vanquished.”** He called for national partnership, dialogue, and reconciliation, while continuing to defend Hezbollah’s weapons and telecommunications network as essential to resistance against Israel.

- **Cabinet compromise:** The factions also accepted a **30-member national-unity Cabinet**: **16 ministers for the Western-backed governing coalition, 11 for Hezbollah and its opposition allies, and three chosen by the president**. The opposition’s 11 seats gave it the “blocking third” needed to veto major Cabinet decisions, while the governing coalition retained a nominal majority. Western-backed Prime Minister **Fouad Siniora** was subsequently designated to lead the new government.

Overall, the May settlement ended an 18-month political deadlock and the immediate armed confrontation, but it did so by granting Hezbollah and its allies substantially greater formal influence without resolving the underlying dispute over Hezbollah’s independent military power.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article explaining how Lebanon ended its 18-month political crisis, why Hezbollah gained veto power in the new government, and what Hassan Nasrallah said about national partnership.
counterfactuals.output:
**Lebanon ends 18-month political crisis with national-unity government**

**BEIRUT —** Lebanon brought an 18-month political confrontation to a formal close with the creation of a national-unity government that gave the Hezbollah-led opposition enough cabinet seats to block major decisions.

The 30-member cabinet, announced in July 2008 under Prime Minister Fouad Siniora and President Michel Suleiman, implemented the central power-sharing provision of the Doha agreement reached by Lebanon’s rival factions in May. Its formation restored a functioning executive after months of institutional paralysis, a prolonged presidential vacancy and the country’s worst internal fighting since the end of the civil war.

Under the agreed formula, the Western- and Saudi-backed parliamentary majority received 16 ministers, the Hezbollah-led opposition received 11, and Suleiman selected three. The allocation was designed to prevent either camp from governing entirely on its own while giving the president a potentially important mediating role.

### How the crisis ended

The political crisis began in November 2006, when Hezbollah and its allies withdrew their ministers from Siniora’s government. The opposition demanded a national-unity cabinet in which it would hold more than one-third of the seats. The governing March 14 coalition rejected that demand, arguing that it would give Hezbollah and its partners the power to paralyze the cabinet.

The dispute spilled into the streets through demonstrations, strikes and a long opposition protest camp in central Beirut. It also left Lebanon without a president after Emile Lahoud’s term expired in November 2007. Although the factions broadly accepted army commander Michel Suleiman as a compromise candidate, parliament repeatedly postponed the presidential vote because they had not settled the shape of the next government and other political questions.

The standoff turned violent in May 2008 after the government moved against Hezbollah’s private telecommunications network and reassigned the security chief at Beirut airport, whom Hezbollah considered an ally. Hezbollah called the decisions a declaration of war. Its fighters and allied gunmen seized control of much of predominantly Sunni west Beirut after clashes with supporters of the governing coalition. Fighting also spread to other parts of the country and killed dozens of people.

The violence changed the political balance and triggered Arab League mediation. Lebanese leaders were brought to Doha, Qatar, where they signed an agreement on May 21.

The Doha accord provided for Suleiman’s immediate election as president, the creation of a 30-member national-unity government and negotiations on a new electoral law. It also called on the factions to refrain from using weapons or violence to achieve political goals.

Parliament elected Suleiman on May 25, ending the six-month presidential vacancy. Forming the cabinet took several more weeks because the factions continued bargaining over individual ministries, particularly sensitive security and service portfolios. Once those allocations were settled, the unity government could finally be announced.

### Why Hezbollah’s camp received veto power

The opposition’s 11 seats amounted to what Lebanese politicians called a “blocking third” or “one-third-plus-one.” Under Lebanon’s constitutional rules, major cabinet decisions require a two-thirds majority. Eleven ministers in a 30-member cabinet could therefore prevent the government from reaching that threshold. Their resignation could also deprive the cabinet of the political and sectarian consensus needed to function.

The veto was not formally awarded to Hezbollah alone. It belonged collectively to the opposition alliance, which included Hezbollah, the Shiite Amal movement and Christian leader Michel Aoun’s Free Patriotic Movement. Hezbollah was nevertheless the most powerful force in that bloc and the principal advocate of the demand.

The arrangement reflected both the opposition’s leverage after the May fighting and the compromise reached in Doha. Hezbollah and its allies had insisted that they needed protection against decisions affecting what they regarded as fundamental interests, especially Hezbollah’s weapons, security apparatus and ability to confront Israel. They argued that Lebanon’s divided political system could not be governed by a simple parliamentary majority.

The March 14 coalition had resisted the blocking-third formula for more than a year, fearing it would allow Hezbollah to obstruct the international tribunal investigating former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri’s assassination, impede security decisions or bring down the cabinet. It eventually accepted the arrangement as the price of ending the violence, electing a president and reopening state institutions.

The majority still held 16 seats, enough to preserve its numerical lead but not enough to take major decisions without support from either the opposition or ministers appointed by Suleiman. The president’s three ministers were intended to serve as a centrist group capable of bridging disputes.

### Nasrallah stresses national partnership

Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah welcomed the new cabinet as an important step toward political stability and described it as an expression of genuine national partnership.

Nasrallah’s central message was that Lebanon could not be ruled through the exclusion of one of its major communities or political camps. He said the unity formula demonstrated that no faction could eliminate the others and that the country had to be governed through cooperation and consensus.

He portrayed the opposition’s participation not simply as a partisan victory but as recognition of a broader principle: major national decisions should be made through partnership rather than imposed by a narrow majority. The government’s formation, he said, opened the way to “true national partnership” and could help close the chapter of confrontation.

That language also reflected Hezbollah’s justification for demanding the blocking third. Nasrallah had long argued that the opposition sought guarantees of participation, not control of the state. Critics, however, said the agreement rewarded Hezbollah for using armed force domestically and converted its military power into political leverage.

### A settlement, but not a resolution of every dispute

The unity cabinet ended the immediate institutional crisis, but it did not settle Lebanon’s deepest divisions. The parties remained at odds over Hezbollah’s independent arsenal, relations with Syria and Iran, the international investigation into Hariri’s killing, and the country’s foreign-policy alignment.

Those issues were deferred to a broader “national dialogue” under President Suleiman. The new government was also charged with preparing for the 2009 parliamentary elections and overseeing implementation of the electoral arrangements negotiated in Doha.

The cabinet therefore represented a truce and a power-sharing mechanism more than a final reconciliation. It restored a president, an executive and a measure of political normality, but it did so by embedding the balance of power that had emerged from the crisis: the March 14 coalition retained the largest share of government, while Hezbollah and its allies gained the veto they had sought since 2006.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Hassan Nasrallah’s address to Hezbollah supporters following the election of consensus presidential candidate Michel Sleiman. Include direct quotations and background on Lebanon’s recent violence and political divisions.
counterfactuals.output:
**Beirut, May 26, 2008 —** Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah welcomed the election of Lebanese army commander Michel Sleiman as president, portraying it as an opportunity to end Lebanon’s prolonged political crisis while insisting that Hezbollah would retain its armed “resistance.”

Speaking by video link to supporters in Beirut’s southern suburbs a day after parliament elected Sleiman, Nasrallah endorsed the Qatari-brokered Doha agreement that cleared the way for the vote. “There are no winners and losers,” he said of the settlement, adding: “The winner is Lebanon, and the loser is sedition.”

Nasrallah rejected demands from the Western- and Saudi-backed governing coalition that Hezbollah disarm. “The resistance and its weapons will remain to confront the enemy, liberate the land and the prisoners, and defend Lebanon, and nothing else,” he said, referring to Israel and to Lebanese prisoners then held in Israeli jails.

He nevertheless acknowledged the danger of using arms in domestic disputes. “The use of weapons internally is a social and national catastrophe,” Nasrallah said. Hezbollah maintained that its fighters had acted only after the government moved against the organization’s private telecommunications network, which Hezbollah described as essential to its defenses against Israel.

Nasrallah also denied that the movement sought to seize the state. “We do not want power, nor do we want to control Lebanon or govern Lebanon,” he said. He called for a national dialogue on a defense strategy that would determine the future relationship between Hezbollah’s arsenal and the Lebanese armed forces.

### Background

Sleiman’s election on May 25 ended a six-month vacancy in the presidency, which had been empty since Émile Lahoud’s term expired in November 2007. Parliament had repeatedly postponed the vote because rival blocs could not agree on a candidate or on the composition of a new government.

The dispute pitted the **March 14 coalition**, led by Sunni politician Saad Hariri and supported by the United States, France and Saudi Arabia, against the **Hezbollah-led opposition**, which included the Shiite Amal movement and Michel Aoun’s largely Christian Free Patriotic Movement and was backed by Syria and Iran.

The crisis turned violent in early May 2008 after Prime Minister Fouad Siniora’s government declared Hezbollah’s private communications network illegal and removed the Beirut airport security chief, whom it considered close to the group. Nasrallah called the measures “a declaration of war.” Hezbollah and allied fighters then overran much of predominantly Sunni west Beirut before handing positions to the army. Fighting also spread to other parts of the country, leaving at least 65 people dead—and, by some later counts, more than 80.

Arab League mediation brought the factions to Doha, where they agreed to elect Sleiman, form a national-unity cabinet giving the opposition enough seats to block major decisions, and adopt a new electoral law. The accord halted the immediate fighting but left the central dispute unresolved: March 14 argued that only the state should possess arms, while Hezbollah said its arsenal remained necessary to deter Israel and defend Lebanon.

**Hezbollah promises not to dominate Lebanon after Doha deal**

**BEIRUT** — Hezbollah has pledged not to use its political and military strength to dominate Lebanon after a Qatari-brokered agreement ended the country’s worst internal fighting since the civil war and cleared the way for the election of a new president.

The Doha agreement, reached after days of negotiations among Lebanon’s rival factions, provided for the formation of a 30-member national unity Cabinet. The Western-backed parliamentary majority will receive 16 seats, the Hezbollah-led opposition 11, and three ministers will be chosen by newly elected President Michel Suleiman.

The arrangement gives the opposition enough Cabinet votes to block major government decisions, addressing one of its central demands. At the same time, the governing coalition retains a simple majority.

Hezbollah leader Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah said the group did not intend to seize control of the state or impose its political program on other Lebanese factions. His comments appeared aimed at easing concerns among supporters of the governing coalition after Hezbollah fighters briefly took control of parts of predominantly Muslim west Beirut during clashes this month.

The fighting, which spread to other parts of the country, killed dozens of people and raised fears of a return to the sectarian violence of Lebanon’s 1975-90 civil war.

Under the Doha accord, the factions also agreed on an electoral law for parliamentary elections and pledged not to use weapons to achieve political goals. The agreement ended an 18-month political crisis that had left Lebanon without a president since November.

Parliament elected Suleiman, the former army commander, as president in a vote welcomed by political leaders across Lebanon and by foreign governments. Supporters portrayed him as a consensus figure capable of maintaining stability and mediating between the rival camps.

The United States and its Arab allies welcomed the election as a step toward restoring Lebanon’s state institutions. Syria and Iran, which support Hezbollah, also praised the agreement and Suleiman’s election.

Suleiman called for national reconciliation and urged Lebanon’s factions to rebuild confidence in state institutions. But deep divisions remain over Hezbollah’s weapons, Lebanon’s relationship with Syria and the balance of power between the governing coalition and the opposition.

The new Cabinet will face the immediate tasks of consolidating the Doha truce, preparing for elections and addressing an economy weakened by years of political paralysis and sporadic violence.
